titulo.texto: Stela of “Los Danzantes” from Monte Albán

frase_gancho.texto: They are not dancing: they are defeated chiefs, carved in stone two thousand five hundred years ago.

puente_narrativo.texto: Monte Albán displayed its power in stone, but it also had a sacred side. Now look for a jade face made from twenty-five green pieces, gazing out from the night.

guion_corto.texto: This slab, almost a meter and a half tall, is one of the so-called “Danzantes” of Monte Albán. The first explorers believed they were dancers, because of their twisted postures. Today they are thought to be portraits of rival chiefs and warriors, captured, stripped naked and sacrificed by the city’s emerging elite. Notice the closed eyes, the limbs bent limp, and the lines that spring from the body: they represent blood. Near each figure there is a glyph, which is probably its name. Monte Albán was founded around the year 500 BC, and this is one of the first things it chose to tell the world: who ruled here.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine a hill. In the year 500 BC, in the center of the Valleys of Oaxaca, several peoples decide to do something enormous: to flatten the top of a mountain by hand in order to found a city. This is Monte Albán. What is remarkable is that they did it in a place with no water nearby, and still the city grew for more than a thousand years. From that summit you command the whole valley, where the three arms of Etla, Zimatlán and Tlacolula meet: whoever sat up here could see anyone coming. And whoever rules in such a place needs to convince others that he cannot be challenged.

Among its first monuments are these slabs. There were hundreds of them, more than three hundred by the usual account, set into a building on the main plaza that we now call the Building of the Danzantes. Each slab shows a naked man, with a slack body and closed eyes, in a pose that looks like a clumsy dance. That is where the name comes from. But the name deceives.

Today they are thought to be the defeated. To strip a chief of his clothing, his jewels and his insignia was to take away his identity: to leave him reduced to a body. Several show mutilations, and from them spring scrolls that represent blood. They are chiefs and warriors of rival peoples, and their image was carved in stone so that no one would forget how it ended for those who opposed the rulers.

Now look at the glyph that accompanies the figure. Each one is the sign of a day in the calendar of two hundred and sixty days, which was used as a personal name. They are among the earliest examples of writing in Mesoamerica: the Zapotecs were already writing names and dates more than two thousand years ago. And this was not the first time they had tried. In San José Mogote, a town in the same valley, an even older slab appeared with the same subject: a sacrificed captive and a sign that names him.

This is propaganda, and of the oldest kind. Two thousand years before the [Stone of Tízoc](mna_s06_tizoc), which you saw in the Mexica Hall, another city was already using stone to say: this is how those who challenge us end. It is the same logic, the same gesture of power, repeated across the centuries. Perhaps that is why it is so unsettling: it reminds us that some things about power have not changed.

Notice also something that cannot be seen at first glance: hardly any two figures share the same posture. Each body was carved differently, with arms and legs at different angles. This suggests that each man was a specific individual, with a name and a biography, and not a generic symbol. Someone took the trouble to remember them one by one, even if only to humiliate them.

Over time, the city’s taste changed: it is thought that several slabs were reused as building stone in later structures, and that is why today some appear cut down or out of place. But this one was preserved whole.

And think about this: this stone was looked at by people coming and going across the most important plaza in the city. It was an open book and a warning at the same time. The Zapotecs had many other ways of telling their world, as you will see shortly, but this was the first they decided to carve in stone.

texto: Look for the closed eyes and the limp arms and legs
Find the glyph beside the figure: it is his name
Look at the lines that spring from the body: what do they represent?

texto.Period: Preclassic, first stage of Monte Albán (Monte Albán I)
texto.Origin: Building of Los Danzantes, Monte Albán, Oaxaca

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Danzantes of Monte Albán are dancers.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are prisoners: rival chiefs and warriors, stripped naked and sacrificed. The name “Danzantes” comes from their twisted postures, which the first explorers mistook for a dance.
